tier_reason: Independent third-party harness is public (NickMRamirez/Proxy-Benchmarks: main.tf, variables.tf, client/run_tests.sh, nginx/nginx.conf, envoy/envoy.yaml, haproxy/haproxy.cfg, *_setup.sh with pinned images envoyproxy/envoy:v1.22.8, nginx:1.22.1, haproxytech/haproxy-ubuntu:2.7.3) but names only AWS m5.xlarge, no CPU model, and is a single run, so not A; issue 5536 is an independent user report without hardware. Both measurements show Envoy slower than NGINX and HAProxy on throughput and mean/median latency.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Not faster. Proxy-Benchmarks (hey, 100,000 requests, 250 connections): Envoy 25,852 req/s vs NGINX 33,506 and HAProxy 39,437 (Envoy 0.77x of NGINX and 0.66x of HAProxy, derived from page data); mean latency 9.5 ms vs 7.2 ms (NGINX) and 6.1 ms (HAProxy); p50 8.9 ms vs 5.7 and 4.1 ms. Envoy is lower only at p90 to p99: p90 12.6 ms vs 14.7 (NGINX) and 13.8 (HAProxy), p95 13.9 vs 18.7 and 18.5, p99 19.5 ms vs 27.5 and 30.6 (29% and 36% lower, derived from page data), but these are measured at 23-34% lower throughput in a closed loop, and the extreme tail is worse: slowest request 111.0 ms vs 67.1 ms (NGINX) and 91.6 ms (HAProxy), with 250 Envoy requests above 56 ms against 5 NGINX requests above 54 ms and 161 HAProxy requests above 55 ms (derived from the page's histograms). Envoy issue 5536 (wrk, 100 connections, 10 threads, 60 s, 4 workers each, nginx backend): Envoy 39,748.81 req/s, 2.73 ms average, 7.10 ms p99, 413.43 ms max vs HAProxy 88,446.34 req/s, 1.14 ms average, 2.20 ms p99, 31.04 ms max.
corrections.workload: Third-party Proxy-Benchmarks suite: hey -n 100000 -c 250 GET from a client VM through each proxy to a jmalloc/echo-server backend VM; all five proxies run as Docker containers on one proxy VM (ports 8000-8004 via -p port mapping) and are tested one after another in a single run_tests.sh pass, one run per proxy, on AWS m5.xlarge instances (Envoy 1.22.8 default concurrency, NGINX worker_processes 3 with upstream keepalive 32, HAProxy 2.7.3 config with no tuning). Second source: Envoy issue 5536, wrk -c100 -t10 -d60s against Envoy (concurrency 4) and HAProxy (nbproc 4) in Docker with host networking in front of an nginx backend.
corrections.caveats: Envoy loses on throughput and on median and mean latency in both sources, and its only favourable numbers (lower p90 to p99 in Proxy-Benchmarks) come from a closed-loop hey run where each proxy is driven at a different request rate: Envoy served 23-34% fewer requests per second, so its tighter p90-p99 is not a like-for-like latency win, and its extreme tail is worse (slowest 111.0 ms vs 67.1 ms NGINX and 91.6 ms HAProxy; a separate cluster of 250 requests at 56-111 ms against 5 NGINX requests above 54 ms, derived from the histograms). The run is one 100,000-request pass lasting 2.5 to 3.9 s per proxy, no warm-up, no repetitions, hey client (coordinated omission possible), all five proxies co-resident as Docker containers on one 4-vCPU proxy VM behind bridge port mapping, proxies configured differently (NGINX worker_processes 3 with upstream keepalive 32; Envoy and HAProxy at default thread counts), and response sizes differ per proxy (253 B Envoy, 126 B NGINX, 140 B HAProxy per request). CPU model not stated (m5.xlarge only). The repo was last updated Aug 2023 (313 stars) and tests Envoy 1.22.8, an old release. The repo owner's GitHub account also hosts HAProxy practice and syntax projects, and a WebSearch snippet lists a Nick Ramirez as HAProxy Technologies Director of Product Marketing on haproxy.com/authors; that this is the same person is not confirmed, but the suite may not be independent of the HAProxy baseline. Issue 5536 is from Jan 2019, hardware not stated, labelled question and closed by the stale bot in Jan 2020; a commenter said the HAProxy config was not optimal, another profiled Envoy and attributed part of the gap to its CPU-intensive HTTP/1 parser, and the reporter noted the nginx backend reached only 60% CPU in the Envoy run. A 2020 HAProxy Technologies Kubernetes ingress benchmark and other write-ups seen in search snippets could not be opened, so they are not used. The Envoy README itself carries no comparison with NGINX or HAProxy.

notes: Numbers on both pages match the record exactly, but Envoy is slower than both baselines on throughput and median/mean latency; the p90-p99 edge is at lower throughput in a closed loop and the max/extreme tail is worse, so not-faster. If kept per house rules, keep tier B with the not-faster shortcoming and the possible HAProxy affiliation of the suite author.

tier_reason: binserve BENCHMARKS.md shows NGINX Default/Tuned and Apache2 wrk rows with CPU model and wrk commands, but no nginx or Apache version, config, MPM, served file or build details; a competitor's quick reference run, not a well-known suite and not reproducible, so C. The 2016 ab gist cross-check is also partial (no hardware, asymmetric tuning).

corrections.caveats: No first-party benchmark in the nginx repository: its README has no performance content and does not mention Apache. The numbers come from the README-linked BENCHMARKS.md of binserve (a competing Rust static server, MIT), which publishes the NGINX and Apache2 rows only as reference baselines for its own results. Tier C: CPU, OS and wrk commands are stated, but nginx and Apache versions, config files, served file, MPM and compiler flags are not given, so it is not reproducible. wrk ran on the same 8-thread laptop CPU (i7-8550U, 15 W mobile part with turbo) as the servers, over localhost. Apache2 ran on port 80 and NGINX on 8081 (possibly an untuned distro Apache against nginx), and the Apache2 row is internally inconsistent: 62,124.60 req/s at a 178.92 ms mean latency would need about 11,100 requests in flight while wrk held 500 connections (Little's law, derived from page data; the NGINX rows give about 480-490, consistent), with stdev 244 ms and max 804 ms, so it reflects stalled or queued connections (e.g. a worker or connection limit) rather than a clean steady-state measurement. Runs are 5 s, best of three. The tuned NGINX row uses an outside tuning guide (denji/nginx-tuning). The cross-check at https://gist.github.com/lukassup/d5ad12753ee13325b177429db01e0258 (last active Dec 2016; nginx 1.11.8 with worker_processes raised to 4 vs stock Apache 2.4.25 event MPM, both from Docker images reached on localhost:8080, single-threaded ab at concurrency 50, no CPU stated) is dated and asymmetrically tuned; nginx served its 612 B welcome page against Apache's 45 B page, httpd had 189 failed requests (length mismatches) in the keep-alive run, and the author's note that nginx's page is the smaller one contradicts the measured lengths; the gap there is only 13-19%. The listed lead in the book (Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed., ch. 4) calls NGINX an HTTP accelerator / cache, with no numbers. Search snippets (not opened pages) point to other 2026 blog comparisons with nginx ahead on static files at high concurrency, but those hosts were unreachable.

notes: All binserve and gist numbers match the record (1.9x and 3.2x derive correctly; +19%/+13% match the gist). Added harness caveats: Apache2 row fails a Little's law check, wrk co-located on a laptop CPU, gist nginx tuned to 4 workers vs stock Apache. Metadata (BSD-2-Clause, 32.0k stars, last commit 2026-10-23) checked.
